title: On-behalf-of flow and retrieval identity
summary: Run retrieval as the user, not as a broad service account. In the Microsoft identity platform the on-behalf-of (OBO) flow lets a middle tier exchange the caller's token for a downstream token that carries the user's rights.
useIf: Each caller has different rights and downstream systems (Search, Graph, a data API) must see who is asking.
avoidIf: The job has no user, such as a scheduled batch. There you need a scoped app identity, not OBO.

explain.md: The **retrieval identity** is the principal under which retrieval runs. A service account with broad read access plus filtering in your code is the confused-deputy shape: every user gets the service's access, and one missed filter leaks. With OBO the middle tier calls a downstream API as the user, so the downstream system enforces the user's rights itself [[r25]].

explain.title: On-behalf-of exchange
explain.alt: The client calls the assistant API with a token for that API. The API sends that token as an assertion to Entra ID and receives a downstream token for the same user, then calls the downstream API with it.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client app
  participant A as Assistant API
  participant E as Entra ID
  participant D as Downstream API
  C->>A: Token whose audience is the assistant API
  A->>E: assertion plus requested_token_use=on_behalf_of
  E-->>A: Token for the downstream API, same user
  A->>D: Call with the user's delegated token

explain.md: The request uses `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer`, `requested_token_use=on_behalf_of`, a `scope` for the downstream API and an `assertion` that is the access token sent to the middle tier. That token must have the middle-tier app as its audience [[r25]]. OBO uses **delegated scopes only, never app roles**, so roles stay attached to the user and never to the app acting for them.

Handle three details. If the downstream API enforces Conditional Access, such as MFA, the token request fails and the middle tier must return that challenge (a 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header) so the client can satisfy it. Never forward a middle-tier token to anything but its intended audience, and never relay it back to the client [[r25]]. In Azure AI Search native ACL queries, the user's Entra token goes in `x-ms-query-source-authorization` while the calling app needs Search Index Data Reader [[r12]].

explain.title: Ingest and query use different identities
explain.md: Ingestion often runs as an app identity with read access to sources, for example SharePoint indexing needs application permissions [[r16]]. Query time must carry the user. Keep the two identities, scopes and logs separate.

explain.title: Token handling (design reasoning)
explain.md: Cache tokens per user and per scope, never share a cache entry between users, never log tokens, and treat any cache TTL on memberships as part of your revocation SLA.

whereToUse: Assistant APIs that call Azure AI Search with native ACLs, Microsoft Graph or a line-of-business API
Systems where per-user audit trails in downstream services matter
Multi-hop agents where each tool call should carry the user's identity
Any design review that finds one service account with read access to everything

use: Rights differ per user and the downstream system can enforce them
You want the downstream audit log to show the real user
You can run a confidential client as the middle tier
avoid: Scheduled jobs with no user present
Downstream systems that cannot accept delegated tokens
Relaying middle-tier tokens to the browser
flips: No interactive user: use a managed identity scoped to the minimum and state the audience of the output
Downstream does not support delegated tokens: map the user to a permission set yourself and enforce it in code
MFA applies downstream: surface the challenge instead of falling back to the app identity

pitfalls.symptom: Every user sees what the service can see
pitfalls.cause: Retrieval ran under an app-only token
pitfalls.fix: Use OBO or token-based enforcement and show where user identity enters the call

pitfalls.symptom: MFA users get empty or generic errors
pitfalls.cause: The middle tier swallowed the Conditional Access challenge
pitfalls.fix: Return the 401 with WWW-Authenticate so the client can step up

pitfalls.symptom: Tokens appear in logs or traces
pitfalls.cause: Request or header logging was left on
pitfalls.fix: Redact authorization headers and log principal ids only

scenarios.title: Interactive assistant, different rights per user
scenarios.situation: A web assistant lets employees search documents in an index with native ACLs and in Graph. Rights differ per user and change daily. The security team wants a per-user audit trail.
unknowns: Does the API run as a confidential client?
scenarios.question: Which retrieval identity do you use?

options.name: A service principal with read on everything, filtering in your code
options.why: Every user then holds the service's access, and a missed filter leaks.
options.tradeoff: Fits public content or a prototype with no per-user rights.

options.name: OBO with delegated scopes, passing the user's token to Search and Graph
options.why: Downstream systems enforce the user's rights and log the user [[r25]].
options.tradeoff: Token plumbing, Conditional Access handling and per-user token caches.

options.name: Service principal plus the user id in a header
options.why: Works when the downstream cannot take delegated tokens.
options.tradeoff: You enforce and audit the mapping yourself.

flips.if: A downstream API cannot accept delegated tokens
flips.then: Pass the user id explicitly and enforce in your own layer.
A service identity is simpler and fine.

scenarios.takeaway: Run retrieval as the user when rights differ per user.

scenarios.title: Nightly summary job with no user
scenarios.situation: A scheduled job produces a daily summary of new documents for a team channel. No user is signed in. Documents come from sources with mixed permissions.
unknowns: Which team members may see which sources?
Can sources be restricted to what the whole channel may read?
scenarios.question: How should the job authenticate?

options.name: Store users' refresh tokens and run as them later
options.why: Offline user impersonation widens exposure and breaks consent.
options.tradeoff: Only appropriate for explicit, user-approved delegated background access.

options.name: A managed identity limited to sources every channel member may read, with the output audience defined
options.why: The job's rights equal the audience's common rights, so the summary cannot reveal more than they could read.
options.tradeoff: The summary omits content that only some members may see.

options.name: A broad service principal that reads everything
options.tradeoff: A leak risk for members who lack rights to some sources.

flips.if: Each reader gets a personal digest
flips.then: Generate it per user with their delegated access.

flips.if: All sources are visible to the whole team

scenarios.takeaway: Without a user, scope the identity to the output audience.

scenarios.title: Downstream requires MFA
scenarios.situation: The assistant calls a data API that has a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA. Some users report that answers silently omit data after a policy change.
unknowns: What error does the token request return?
Does the client handle claims challenges?
scenarios.question: How do you fix it?

options.name: Return the Conditional Access challenge (401 with WWW-Authenticate) so the client can step up
options.why: The user can satisfy MFA and the call then runs as them [[r25]].
options.tradeoff: The client must handle claims challenges.

options.name: Catch the error and retry with the app identity
options.why: It bypasses the policy and widens access.

options.name: Show a generic error and ask the user to sign in again
options.tradeoff: Poor experience and may loop without the claims challenge.

flips.then: Redirect the user to a sign-in page that triggers MFA.

flips.if: The data does not need Conditional Access
flips.then: Relax the policy for that API instead of working around it.

scenarios.takeaway: Surface the challenge and never fall back to the app identity.

quiz.q: Which statement about the OBO flow is correct?
options: The middle tier receives the app roles of its own app registration for the downstream call
It uses delegated scopes only, so roles stay with the user and not the app
The token sent as the assertion can have any audience
It lets the browser reuse the middle-tier token directly
quiz.explain: OBO exchanges the user's token for a downstream token with delegated scopes and never app roles. The assertion must have the middle-tier app as its audience, and middle-tier tokens must not be relayed to clients.

items: The client calls the assistant API with a token whose audience is that API
The API posts the token as the assertion with requested_token_use=on_behalf_of
Entra ID returns a downstream token for the same user
The API calls the downstream API with that token
quiz.explain: The client token arrives first, the middle tier exchanges it at the token endpoint, receives a downstream token and uses it to call the downstream API.

flashcards.back: The principal under which retrieval runs: the caller (delegated token) or a service account. It decides what the index or source returns.

flashcards.front: Why does OBO use delegated scopes only?
flashcards.back: So roles stay attached to the user and never to the app acting on their behalf, which prevents a user gaining rights they should not have.

flashcards.front: What must the middle tier do when downstream Conditional Access demands MFA?
flashcards.back: Surface the challenge to the client (a 401 with WWW-Authenticate) so the user can step up. Never fall back to the app identity.
